title: How do online retailers make money, and what matters in an e-commerce case?
description: E-commerce economics for case interviews: traffic, conversion, average order value, returns, fulfilment cost and customer acquisition, with a worked funnel…
hook: Online retailers make money when the margin on what customers keep is larger than the cost of attracting them, delivering each order and handling returns. An e-commerce case usually tests two things: funnel thinking (visitors × conversion × order value) to find where revenue is won or lost, and order-level economics to check whether each sale actually makes money once acquisition, fulfilment and returns are counted.
body:
The funnel

Revenue = visitors × conversion rate × average order value (AOV). Each piece can be broken down further: visitors by source (paid search, social ads, email, direct), conversion by step (product page, basket, checkout, payment) and by device, AOV by items per order and price per item. Separating new and repeat customers is often the most useful split, because they behave and cost so differently.

A worked example: where to focus

An illustrative online store has 1M visitors a month, a 2% conversion rate and a $60 AOV: 20,000 orders and $1.2M of sales a month.

  • Raising conversion to 2.5% adds 1M × 0.5% × $60 = $300k a month.
  • Raising AOV by 10% to $66 adds 20,000 × $6 = $120k a month.

On these numbers conversion is the bigger lever, so you would start with product pages and checkout. But sales are not profit. Suppose 20% of orders come back for a full refund and the product margin is 35%. Of the $1.2M, only $960k is kept, producing $336k of gross profit before fulfilment, acquisition, return handling and overhead.

The economics of one order

Build a contribution bridge for an average $60 order, using illustrative costs:

LinePer order
Revenue kept after 20% returns ($60 × 80%)$48.00
Product cost on items kept (65% of $48)−$31.20
Return handling ($7 × 20% of orders)−$1.40
Picking, packing and delivery−$8.00
Payment fees (2% of $60)−$1.20
Contribution per order$6.20

Now add acquisition. If winning a new customer through paid ads costs $25, the first order loses about $19. The customer has to place about four orders ($25 ÷ $6.20 ≈ 4) before the business earns back what it spent. That is why repeat rate matters as much as conversion, and why a campaign that brings one-off bargain hunters can grow sales while destroying value.

The hidden costs

  • Customer acquisition: paid search and social ads get more expensive as you push for more volume.
  • Fulfilment: picking, packing and delivery are a fixed-ish cost per order, so small orders are often unprofitable. Minimum order values and free-delivery thresholds exist for this reason.
  • Returns: in categories like fashion, where customers order several sizes, returns can wipe out the profit on many orders.

Typical e-commerce case questions

  • Why have conversion or sales fallen? (walk the funnel by step, device and traffic source)
  • Why have returns costs doubled?
  • Should we offer free delivery?
  • How can we lower customer acquisition cost?
  • Should a store-based retailer push harder online, or a marketplace add a new category?

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Sales are down, so we should spend more on online ads and SEO."
Strong: "I'd split the decline into traffic, conversion and order value first. If traffic is flat but conversion fell, I'd look at checkout by device and week. If the fall is on mobile since we changed payment options, that's the place to start."

The strong answer forms a specific hypothesis and names the data that would test it.

Common mistakes

  • Stopping at revenue. A conversion win means little if the extra orders are small, heavily discounted or mostly returned.
  • Ignoring returns. Always ask for sales after returns and the cost of each return.
  • Comparing conversion rates across categories. 3% in one category is not better than 2% in another if margins and baskets differ.
  • Treating CAC as a one-order cost. Acquisition cost should be judged against the customer's lifetime of orders (see unit economics).

Practise

1. A store has 500k visits a month, converts 3% and has an $80 AOV. Which is worth more: raising conversion by half a point, or raising AOV by $10?

Show the answer

Sales today: 500k × 3% × $80 = $1.2M. Conversion to 3.5% adds 500k × 0.5% × $80 = $200k. AOV of $90 adds 15,000 orders × $10 = $150k. Conversion wins on revenue, but check which is cheaper to achieve and what each does to margin.

2. In the order bridge above, the return rate rises from 20% to 30%. What happens to contribution per order?

Show the answer

Revenue kept: $60 × 70% = $42. Product cost: 65% × $42 = $27.30. Return handling: $7 × 30% = $2.10. Delivery $8 and payment $1.20 are unchanged. Contribution: $42 − $27.30 − $2.10 − $8 − $1.20 = $3.40, down 45% from $6.20.

3. With $6.20 of contribution per order, a $25 CAC and customers ordering three times a year, how long does a new customer take to pay back?

Show the answer

$25 ÷ $6.20 ≈ 4 orders. At three orders a year, that is about 16 months, provided the customer is still buying.

Where to practise next

Try the LeafCart case on a fast grocery delivery business with lots of orders and no profit, and the CraneParcel case on failed deliveries. For the store-based side of retail, read grocery retail cases.
